entries.title: The 4 Best Car Phone Mounts I’ve Tried (2026): Belkin, Andery, Andobil
entries.summary: The best car phone holders keep your phone firmly in place while never getting in your line of sight. I took a dozen on road trips this summer to find the best.
entries.content:
A car phone mount is no longer an option—it's a necessity. Nearly every US state restricts cell phone use while driving (we see you, Montana!), and most require full hands-free operation. The best car phone mounts offer an easy view of your phone's screen without blocking your view of the road, hold your phone securely, and keep vibration to a minimum.

I've spent weeks and hundreds of miles testing car phone holders for iPhones and Android alike, on busy freeways and on potholed city roads. What I found is that the best car phone mounts aren't necessarily expensive or name brands: They're just smartly designed.

The best car phone mount for an iPhone is almost always a secure MagSafe mount. The one I keep in my car when I'm not testing other mounts is a sturdy, compact Andery suction mount ($36) that holds preternaturally fast to both my phone and dash but can also be mounted to a window. My favorite mechanical car phone holder for Android phones is a sturdy, versatile, ball-joint mount from Andobil ($30) that affixes tightly to a car's dash, windshield, or air vents.

Here are the best car phone mounts for each car and phone type. See also WIRED's guides to the Best USB Car Chargers, Best Portable Jump Starters, Best iPhone Cases and Accessories, Best MagSafe Accessories, and Best Wireless Phone Chargers.

Best Car Phone Mount for iPhones and Qi2 Phones

The world is full of bulky phone mounts that block your view of the road, inflexible phone mounts that only allow for horizontal or vertical mounting, weak suction cups, and kinda mid MagSafe attachments. And then there's this innovatively designed, wonderfully compact dash and window mount from Andery.

On flat surfaces, the nano-gel suction cup holds fast like Hodor at the door. The 22-magnet MagSafe ring allows airflow to avoid overheating, but it also holds stronger than most comparable Qi2 magnets. And unlike bulky plastic mounts, the Andery's aluminum-arm, stainless steel ring keeps a low profile and interferes minimally with one's line of sight. In fact, when affixed to my dash, this device doesn't block my view of the road at all. The ring rotates 360 degrees. The two-joint arm can either fold tightly to the mount or extend outward. No other mount I've tested combines all of these virtues.

But note you'll need a relatively flat surface to get a good bond with the suction cup. I've also seen some reports that the suction cup can lose adhesion over time if repeatedly re-mounted (and it's cussedly difficult to remove in the first place, though it leaves no residue when you do). Non-Qi2-compatible Android phones will need a MagSafe case to be compatible with this car phone holder. But if your phone has a magnet or a magnetic case, this is the simplest and most effective car phone mount I know, and it performs leagues better than other similarly designed car mounts like this one from Acer.

Note also that Andery offers a Qi2-compatible phone charger version at the expense of airflow. I haven't tested this variant yet.

Best Universal Car Phone Mount

Mechanical mounts like this one from Andobil—with holders that can be slid in sideways to securely grip the phone—are flexible for a broad range of phones and don't require MagSafe technology. But they're also mostly bulky, making them a less preferred option as a windshield or dashboard mount because this will block your field of vision.

Among all similar devices I've tested, this one from newer Chinese company Andobil is the most compact I've tested when not in use, while still offering a lot of flexibility. The nanogel suction cup on its dash mount is one of the most stable I've tested (almost aggressively stuck on, to be honest). And the extendable arm, while plastic, feels less cheap and breakable than other models. The kit also comes with an air vent mount, whose three-point design makes it among the most stable vent mounts I've tested and allows you to maneuver the phone so it does not block the vent.

This mechanical car phone holder is hard to call aesthetic. It's essentially a pad with a gripper on the side. But the grips extend to accommodate even larger phones and are able to keep the phone in place even during vigorous shaking. (If you're wondering whether I place phones in these phone mounts, and then come at them like they're a shake weight? I do.) The release button's a little awkwardly placed, and Andobil's marketing about “military standards” is a little silly on a low-cost device made with thermoplastics. But after I watched other suction cups wilt in summer heat, this Andobil's still going strong.

★ A Great, Low-Cost Air Vent Mount: If you're mounting only to your air vent, the Vanva air vent phone mount ($13) is among the cheapest mounts of any kind that I've tested, while ranking among the most secure mechanical mounts. (Actually, I like the mechanical phone holder a bit better than Andobil's.) The lockable clamp affixes easily and securely to most vertical or horizontal-slatted vents—and unlike hook-based vent mounts, it's easy to install and remove. The multi-joint ball arm can be maneuvered so you don't lose airflow from the vent, and the adjustable grips that lock in your phone can be released with a simple button press. This Vanva is a relatively flimsy plastic device, so I don't rule out that it might break someday. But its inexpensive replacement cost makes this an acceptable risk.

Best Car Phone Mount With Charger

Look, I'll be honest: I have mixed feelings about chargers on car phone mounts. The mount will have to be plugged into a car charger anyway—and at that point, I might as well just plug in the phone directly, which will usually lead to faster charging.

But convenience is in the eye of the beholder, and many people prefer to just leave the car mount plugged permanently into a car charger so they never have to worry about their phone draining while navigating on a mapping app. For y'all, here's the car mount from ESR, which offers decently fast 15-watt charging and a cooling fan to mitigate phone overheating.

The suction was effective when attached to both my window and dash, and the device is compact enough to not much hinder my field of view. Charging speed is merely moderate, enough to charge an older iPhone in a couple of hours. ESR also offers a faster-charging Qi2.2 device for twice the money, though I have not tested it.

★ A Good, Stylish Vent Charging Mount: Most vent chargers plant themselves directly into the airflow of your vent. But not all of them do. WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu recommends the Peak Design Car Vent Mount ($100). The mount stays secure on the vent, but an arm allows the charger a little distance from the vent. It's also a little bit stylish, a rarity for vent mounts. If you're using a Pixel or Samsung phone, we also like Peak Design's MagSafe phone cases.

Best Minimalist Car Phone Mount

Most people don't overwhelmingly want their car vent mount to be a defining feature in their car's interior. This Belkin takes this notion to the extreme. This silver and black air vent mount is minimalist, svelte, and—dare I say—almost classy. It grips phones surprisingly securely for a phone mount without feet to support the phone's bottom, according to WIRED reviewer Simon Hill, and you can rotate easily from portrait to landscape. There's also a handy rubber clip to hold charging cables in place. Just note that this will not be the best option for larger or heavier phones.

★ For larger phones: The Kenu Airframe Pro ($30) has a similar design but is built to accommodate thicker cases and larger phones, noted WIRED tester Simon Hill. The ball-and-socket joint allows 360-degree rotation and also lets you angle your phone for better viewing. It's a bit less sleek, however.

How I Test and Select Car Phone Mounts

Car phone mounts are and are not a sensitive technology. Bulky mounts can block your field of view while driving. And it's a genuine safety hazard if your car mount, or your phone, falls on the floor while you're driving down the freeway.

Every phone mount I and other WIRED testers recommend has been road-tested against this possibility, driven for hours on the road, and on long road trips, over sometimes bumpy roads. Often, I kept as many as eight devices at a time glued to my dash, windshield, and vents so that my car looked like a dollar-store communications center. For the most recent round of testing, this included multiple days of relatively humid, 90-degree Fahrenheit heat.

I pulled suction cups off of dashboards and windshields, over and over, to see if suction cups wore out the first time you had to move a device—or if the cups left residue on the windshield. I tested using multiple models of iPhone, a long folding Motorola Razr, and a large-model Nokia, onto each mount to see how it held up—with or without bulky cases.

I clamped each phone in and out repeatedly, to see how easy it is to remove a phone from the mount. I also turned each mount upside down and shook vigorously to see how violent I had to be to shake the phone loose from its mooring.

Where chargers were involved, I tested the charging capacity with ammeters and phone apps, as well as simply by marking how long it took to charge my phone compared to other chargers. I also tested the MagSafe charging speed vs. the speed if I'd just plugged the phone directly into my preferred USB car charger. (The USB always wins, for multiple reasons.)

For the most recent round of testing, I tested a dozen phone mounts during a sticky summer, selecting both best-selling and best-recommended mounts from both well-known brands and a new breed of hyper-specialized brands like Andobil and Andery that have made their name only on car phone mounts. My colleague Simon Hill likewise tested a dozen mounts in a previous round of testing.

Can Android Phones Use MagSafe and Qi2-Compatible Mounts?

MagSafe is a great technology for the more than half of cell phone owners in the US who use Apple products. The best phone mounts, with the fewest compromises, are pretty much all magnetic mounts.

But alas, most makers of Android phones have been more resistant to adding magnetic mounting capability. The Google Pixel 10 is an exception and offers built-in magnets and native Qi2-compatible charging support. Other phone makers, like Samsung, offer MagSafe-compatible cases for newer models like the Galaxy S26 series.

Some makers of MagSafe mounts offer little stick-on devices meant to affix to your non-magnetic phone. Don't bother with these; they don't work that well and don't stay affixed for long. If you'd like the convenience of a magnetic mount, you're going to have to get a MagSafe-compatible case for your phone. And for this, I refer you to WIRED's guide to the Best MagSafe Accessories.

Honorable Mentions

Belkin 15W MagSafe Mount for $80: This Belkin MagSafe charger and vent mount is an older device we've recommended previously as a top pick—with a secure magnet pad that offers 15-watt Qi2 charging. The mount positions itself in the air vent and blocks airflow a bit, but on summer days with the air-conditioner running, this positioning can help cool your phone while it charges. It's also a little bit sleek but also a bit on the spendy side for what it offers.

Andobil MagSafe Air Vent Mount for $37: This vent-mounted MagSafe device looks like a charger but isn't. The mount's broad, flat surface does stabilize the phone a bit. But in trade, it blocks airflow both to the phone and from the air vent. For these reasons, it's not really my favorite design. But the magnet is strong enough to hold the phone in place, and the vent mount is also stable.

iOttie iTap 3 Air Vent Holder for $16: This compact vent mount from iOttie is low-cost, and the MagSafe mount is strong enough. I can hold this thing upside down and shake it without dislodging my phone. But there's very little range of motion, and the phone can only be mounted where it'll block airflow from the vent. I also tend not to favor mounting mechanisms that use hooks, because it can make the mounts more difficult to remove when needed—though for unusual air vent geometries, the hook might be the only style of vent mount that works.

iOttie One Touch Dash and Windshield Mount for $28: This dash and windshield mount from iOttie was a favorite of WIRED tester Simon Hill when he tested it two years ago. But there's been a design update and some reports of durability issues, so until we test the newest model, I'm leaving this in the honorable mentions.

Vanmass Car Phone Holder for $40: Similar to the Andobil I recommend as a top pick, this Vanmass is a ball-socket mount with options for air vent or dashboard/windshield mounting. But it's a bit bulkier than the Andobil, and the air vent mount is a hook-based mount—which I tend to find more difficult to remove. The suction cup on the dash/windshield mount is ridiculously strong and is unllikely to dislodge even on hot days—and didn't leave residue when I removed it. But while Vanmass advertises “military-grade” tech, whatever this means for a phone mount, the plastic felt a bit flimsy, especially on a vacuum locking mechanism for the suction cup.

Bokilino Car Cup Mount for $16: This is a different sort of phone mount than most I tested: It affixes to a standard cup holder and holds up your phone like a liberty torch from atop a bendable gooseneck stem. This is all well and good when you're driving solo, notes WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, but during longer trips with family, it takes up a much-needed cup holder, and the stem can get in the way. In most cars, you'll have to look a bit too far away from the road to see the screen.

Not Recommended

Acer Gadget Car Phone Mount for $28: This little car mount from Acer mirrored the design of my top-pick Andery but fell far short on performance. The suction cup pretty much walked off the job after I removed and replaced it once, the magnet isn't as strong, and the mounting arm is shorter and doesn't rotate. There's no particular reason to buy it in a world where the Andery exists.

iOttie iTap 3 Dash and Windshield Mount for $25: MagSafe car phone mounts from iOttie have one chief merit: The magnet is strong and secure, unlikely to dislodge on even the bumpiest roads. But alas, the same cannot be said for the suction cup on this bulky dash and windshield mount, which gave up the ghost on a hot day.

Scosche Magic Mount for $13: This is maybe the most compact, low-cost MagSafe device I tested. Its S-branded design is both unobtrusive and winningly inscrutable: It looks like a talisman Jor-El might have brought back from Krypton. It's also the one with the weakest magnet. My iPhone lurched off at minor provocations.

iOttie Wireless 2 Qi Charging Phone Mount for $50: Don't mistake “Wireless 2 Qi Charger” for a Qi2 charger. A couple of years back, this MagSafe charging mount was a top pick for WIRED, but the charging is now a bit sluggish by modern standards.

entries.title: The County Prosecutors Who Became ICE Informants
entries.summary: Illinois prosecutors shared defendants’ personal data with federal immigration agents without criminal warrants, public disclosure, or legislative oversight.
entries.content:
This story was produced in partnership with Injustice Watch, a nonprofit newsroom in Chicago focused on the court system.

Rolando Perez Samayoa had come to the US in 2023 seeking safety. Fleeing violence in Mexico, he’d first planned to make a life in Alabama but had been told that Illinois would protect immigrants like him. “There’s some kind of law there,” he said. “It’s supposed to be a sanctuary.”

He was referring to the state’s 2017 TRUST Act, which was meant to keep local law enforcement out of federal deportation efforts. Samayoa made his way to southern Illinois and found work cleaning a factory. After a DUI arrest in Marion County last October, Samayoa said, he attended his hearings—a fact confirmed by court records.

In late January, John Christeson, an assistant state’s attorney in the office prosecuting the case, emailed an agent with Homeland Security Investigations, a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, about Samayoa. The message included his date of birth, an upcoming court date, and where he lived: Centralia, Illinois.

“Ok, we’ll take care of it, thank you,” the federal agent, Sergio Fulgencio, wrote back minutes later. Two days later, he wanted to know more: “Do you have any reports on this guy?”

Christeson sent him the police report and related tickets. Three weeks later, federal agents apprehended Samayoa outside his home. They hauled off his 17-year-old son, too.

The exchange is among dozens of emails reviewed by Injustice Watch that reveal a pattern of consequential collaboration between county prosecutors and federal immigration agencies across Illinois during the first 15 months of President Donald Trump’s second term.

State’s attorneys offices in 1 out of every 6 Illinois counties acted as valuable assets of federal immigration enforcement, sharing sensitive personal data about the people they were prosecuting without criminal warrants, public disclosure, or legislative oversight and with no accounting of how often it happened or who was affected.

Sometimes, prosecutors volunteered information on their own. Other times, they simply answered when Department of Homeland Security agents came calling. The correspondence crossed party lines and included everyone from paralegals to elected state’s attorneys. The collaboration typically happened without the knowledge of defendants or their attorneys.

The TRUST Act bars police and other agencies from helping federal agents deport people absent a federal criminal warrant. But the law doesn’t squarely answer whether prosecutors and their staff are bound by those same restrictions.

Since Trump took office for the second time, his administration has ramped up immigration enforcement, detention, and deportation, and ICE has visibly displayed its enforcement at worksites, front yards, and courthouses. In response, states including New York have joined Illinois and more than a dozen others in barring local police and sheriffs from helping with federal immigration enforcement. But the scale of prosecutor collaboration in Illinois—which is one of the largest sanctuary states and is often cited as a national model—raises questions about the limitations of state laws to protect immigrants.

Injustice Watch filed Freedom of Information Act requests with all 102 Illinois state’s attorney’s offices and drew on records from federal and circuit courts. Together, those internal emails and case files ran more than 5,000 pages. The documents reveal that prosecutors shared much more than just names. Their emails contain photographs. Home addresses. The date and time a defendant was due in court or set to leave jail—the exact window for ICE to make an arrest.

Eleven offices didn’t respond; some produced records only after Injustice Watch sued them under FOIA. The rest remain in litigation.

And the written record may be only part of the story. Messages with phrases like “Thank you for taking my call” point to conversations no records requests could follow.

None of it was inevitable. Dozens of Illinois county prosecutors, faced with the same federal pressure, claimed they had no record of contact with ICE, and at least one made a point of shutting it out—suggesting every act of collaboration was a choice.

And the choices had consequences: People flagged to ICE were detained and deported, tearing families apart.

DHS did not answer questions about how its agents work with local officials in Illinois.

Antonio Gutierrez, who cofounded the advocacy group Organized Communities Against Deportations, was among those who pushed for the TRUST Act. Residents wanted “to trust in local police, in local prosecutors, in the criminal justice system, to be fully separated from immigration and deportation enforcement,” Gutierrez said.

The records revealed in Injustice Watch’s investigation, Gutierrez said, prove that trust was never warranted.

The Ones Who Were Willing

Twenty minutes after flagging Samayoa, Marion County’s Christeson emailed Fulgencio again.

“I’ve got another potential,” he wrote, flagging a man with a local warrant who had been arrested on an unrelated charge in Missouri.

Fulgencio replied that agents were already tracking the man on a civil removal order—a deportation order from an immigration court—and asked whether the county warrant should take priority.

“Our warrant will not take priority over removal,” Christeson answered.

Fulgencio wrote back just 34 minutes later: “He’s in ICE Custody awaiting removal.”

Christeson didn’t respond to questions about his correspondence with Fulgencio, nor did his boss, Marion County State’s Attorney Tim Hudspeth.

Criminal cases offer protections that immigration proceedings don’t: Prosecutors must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and attorneys are appointed to defendants who can’t afford one. Removal proceedings are civil: There’s no right to an appointed lawyer, and the government can establish deportability on “clear and convincing evidence,” a lower legal standard.

Spencer Reynolds, an attorney with the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and a former Department of Homeland Security lawyer, said that because deportation is an easier path than prosecution, some local officials might be tempted to use it to “clear their docket”—a move that “risks undermining the rights people have in the criminal proceeding context.” Once a defendant is turned over to ICE, the criminal case—and the protections it affords the accused—fall away.

In several counties, prosecutors reached out only once or twice. Some local prosecutor’s offices did nothing more than ask immigration officials whether a defendant was already in federal custody but may have put the person on ICE’s radar in the asking.

According to documents reviewed by Injustice Watch, contact happened more often in DuPage County in Chicago’s western suburbs, where 1 in 5 residents were born abroad. Staff there contacted federal immigration agents more than any other prosecutor’s office in the state. Staffers answered ICE’s requests for information and offered specific cases for federal agents to pursue.

In April 2025, for example, a Customs and Border Protection officer based at O’Hare International Airport asked an assistant prosecutor for records tied to a voter fraud investigation. The request was an administrative subpoena—issued by DHS, not by a judge. On its own it carried little weight: If the office refused, DHS would have to go to federal court and attempt to enforce it.

Ninety minutes later, the prosecutor sent the voting records of two county residents.

DuPage State’s Attorney Bob Berlin said his office reviewed the subpoena like any other before producing the records CBP sought. Its other contacts with immigration agents, he said, were permitted under the TRUST Act’s criminal investigation carve-out, which allows cooperation with federal agencies—including Homeland Security—in such investigations.

Sometimes, the collaboration crossed county lines.

In central Illinois, Menard County State’s Attorney Gwendolyn Thomas contacted federal immigration agents on at least five occasions, often asking whether a defendant was “on a deportation list” in order to assess flight risk, and sometimes sharing details about the men she was prosecuting, including when one might be released from jail.

She also pointed colleagues in neighboring Cass and Mason counties to Homeland Security investigator Kevin Parks. Prosecutors subsequently wrote to Parks on their own, telling him Thomas had shared his contact information.

Cass County State’s Attorney Craig Miller—who shared information about three defendants with federal agents—declined to comment. Thomas didn’t respond to questions about her communications with agents or about steering other prosecutors to Parks.

Mason County State’s Attorney Zachary Bryant told Injustice Watch that the information his office had received from Homeland Security “was helpful in obtaining appropriate identification for purposes of obtaining a valid criminal history for the defendant,” even though records show Parks shared information regarding the defendant’s immigration history, not her criminal history. Bryant did not respond to questions about the discrepancy.

None of the state’s attorneys who responded to Injustice Watch’s questions described the contact they and their staff had made as a mistake or the work of a rogue employee; like DuPage County’s Berlin, most defended their practices outright.

“It is very common that information is shared between agencies in the criminal justice system, including those in law enforcement,” wrote Kendall County State’s Attorney Eric Weis, whose office sent a man’s records to a Detroit ICE office for use in immigration court proceedings.

In Kane County, where staffers asked Customs and Border Protection to identify three people through facial recognition, State’s Attorney Jamie Mosser called it “a standard investigatory technique used throughout all of law enforcement.”

The Ones Who Said No

In response to records requests, more than half of Illinois state’s attorneys offices said they had no record of contact with ICE since Trump returned to office. Some offices chose not to collaborate out of internal practice, some out of a commitment to community trust.

In Lake County, State’s Attorney Eric Rinehart spent months hardening his office against immigration enforcement. He circulated the Illinois attorney general’s guidance on complying with the TRUST Act to police chiefs and told the county’s public defender to report any TRUST Act violations, adding that he not only enforced the law, he “happen[ed] to agree with it such that I hope it is widely followed in letter and spirit.”

“When people are afraid to come to court, for any reason,” he wrote to state lawmakers in October, “we cannot make our communities safe, we cannot find the truth, and we cannot achieve justice.”

Rinehart also issued a written policy barring ICE officials from the private areas of his office without a warrant signed by a judge.

In southern Illinois, Jackson County treated questions from federal agents the way they would any other: as FOIA requests, answered with redactions under the state’s public records law.

Unprecedented

Illinois has made repeated promises to its residents about the way it treats immigrants.

Then-governor Bruce Rauner, a Republican, signed the TRUST Act with bipartisan support at a packed restaurant in Little Village, the Chicago neighborhood at the heart of the city’s Mexican community, months after Trump first took office in 2017 promising mass deportations. Among the attendees were law enforcement officials who wanted to assure the public that immigrants had no reason to fear contacting the police.

In 2021, Governor JB Pritzker called Illinois “the most welcoming state in the United States.” In June 2025, he flew to Washington to defend his position before a hostile House committee. In December, as ICE swept people up outside hearings, he also signed a law in Little Village, this one barring civil immigration arrests within 1,000 feet of a courthouse. The idea that the Trump administration would keep people from attending court, he said at the signing, “boggles the mind.”

But the courthouse law was written to stop the agent waiting on the sidewalk, not the prosecutor inside.

Nearly all the defense attorneys whose clients appear in the records obtained by Injustice Watch said they had no idea prosecutors were sharing case information with federal immigration agents. They spoke on the condition of anonymity, several citing concern about straining relationships with the prosecutors they face in court, others pointing to cases that are still pending.

Legal scholars described the collaboration between federal immigration agents and local prosecutors as unprecedented.

“I cannot recall a single instance in my past practice where an individual within the state’s attorney’s office shared information with ICE,” said University of Kentucky assistant law professor Matthew Boaz.

Still, he said in an email, “the sentiment of the TRUST Act—separating state/local criminal law enforcement from federal civil immigration enforcement—would seem to include any actor within the criminal legal system.”

Prosecutors themselves couldn’t agree on whether the TRUST Act applied to them.

Some said their offices are bound by it. The act covers law enforcement agencies; DuPage County’s Berlin said that includes him and his staff.

“The State’s Attorney’s Office is charged with enforcement of state, county, and municipal laws,” he said. “Therefore, the law applies to my office.”

Others said the law doesn’t reach them. Lake County’s Rinehart said his office doesn’t arrest or detain people, so it isn’t a law enforcement agency as defined by the act. Yet Rinehart said his office declines to collaborate with federal immigration enforcement regardless.

These two offices staked out the clearest positions, landing on opposite sides of the question—and on opposite ends of the spectrum of collaboration. Berlin said his office was bound by the TRUST Act, but it contacted federal immigration officials more than any other. Rinehart said his office wasn’t bound by it, yet shut ICE out entirely. (Neither office tracks its contact with ICE. While police departments and sheriff’s offices must file annual TRUST Act compliance reports, state’s attorneys aren’t required to do so.)

Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, the state’s chief legal officer, didn’t resolve the question.

“Applying the TRUST Act in practice requires state and local enforcement to navigate complex interactions in circumstances that are not always clear-cut,” he said in a statement, without answering whether county prosecutors are bound by the law he enforces.

Pritzker didn’t respond to questions about whether the TRUST Act binds prosecutors, whether the state should track their contacts with ICE, or whether Illinois has kept its promises to its residents.

For Samayoa, the question of whom the law binds is beside the point.

Whatever idea he had about Illinois being a sanctuary ended in February, when ICE agents descended on him in his front yard as he was stepping out to grab a belated birthday dinner. He said eight agents pointed their guns at his teen son, who was trying to reach him as ICE moved in.

“Everything was going smoothly until his 17-year-old son thought he would help his dad out by trying to run over the agents,” Homeland Security’s Fulgencio wrote to Marion County’s Christeson after the incident. “Ended up damaging a vehicle. So now [his son’s] going with him.”

Samayoa denied that his son tried to run over the agents. DHS defended the way its agents handled the arrest.

“ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers,” a spokesperson said in a statement. “Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training.”

Samayoa and his son were taken to St. Louis, where he said he felt pressured to agree to leave the country rather than fight his case. He directed his son to do the same. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed both father and son “accepted a voluntary departure.” Within hours, both were on a plane to Texas.

After one night in an El Paso hotel, Samayoa said, he and his son were escorted across the border into Ciudad Juarez, where he destroyed all immigration paperwork he had with him—vowing to never return to the US. DHS confirmed both were removed from the US on Feb. 25.

Father and son spent time in a shelter before scraping together bus fare to their native state of Chiapas. Back in Illinois, the rest of the family had to raise their own fare south; two months passed before they were all together again.

When Injustice Watch reached Samayoa, he said he didn’t know that a prosecutor had shared information about him with federal immigration authorities before the raid. He said he’d warn the community he left behind in Illinois: Showing up for prosecutors could mean showing up for ICE.

entries.title: Optoma GT2400HDR Review: Ace Projector for Golf Simulation
entries.summary: The Optoma GT2400HDR laser projector is great for setting up a driving range in your living room, but mediocre video quality makes it less appealing for home entertainment.
entries.content:
Indoor golf simulators aren't easy to set up, and they aren't inexpensive. It starts with a home cinema projector, but you also need a wide, open space for swinging clubs, a backdrop with netting, and a gaming laptop or desktop to run the software. I was on a mission to see if I could do this much more cheaply with an affordable projector.

I accomplished my goal successfully by building around the Optoma GT2400HDR short-throw projector. I skipped the most expensive components, like the backdrop and the clubs. Instead, I used a gaming laptop and controller I already owned, and played EA Sports PGA Tour, which is included with my PC Game Pass Ultimate account. While the projector isn’t a bad option for playing golf at home on the cheap, it’s not ideal for watching movies and TV shows. It also struggles with high-octane games, and it doesn’t even include a smart TV platform.

Made for Indoor Driving Ranges

Optoma describes the GT2400HDR as a laser-based short-throw projector designed for gaming, entertainment, and golf simulation (the latter being my main intention). It can project a screen size from 30 to 300 inches at Full HD 1080p (1920 x 1080) resolution. My goal in creating an indoor driving range was to keep costs as low as possible, so I planned to use my Xbox controller with a gaming laptop and play on a 100-inch screen while still feeling like I was out on the links. For a golf game, you can get by with a midrange computer or even use a golf sim app on your iPad. (To do that, you’ll need to cast to a device that supports AirPlay or connect through HDMI via an adapter.)
